nasa_hrp_risks.full_title: Risk of In-Mission Injury and Performance Decrements and Long-term Health Effects due to Dynamic Loads
nasa_hrp_risks.risk_statement: Given the exposure to the range of anticipated dynamic loads that might be applied to crew within the hostile closed environment of a spacecraft and/or surface vehicle (suited or unsuited) could result in injury to the crew, resulting in a possibility that mission task performance would be impaired, or tasks could not be performed. HSRB State of Knowledge Standards and vehicle design requirements are based on automotive and military environments and operational protocols; they are also partially tailored to the spaceflight environment. However, these do not adequately mitigate the risk of injury due to the unique spaceflight environment. Current analytical tools are used outside of their validation conditions and have been shown to under predict Soyuz landing injury. Injury due to standing during dynamic phases of flight is poorly documented in the literature and little data are available. Injury assessment reference values have not been validated due to limited load and injury data from Soyuz landings. Mitigation Strategy The Occupant Protection Team at NASA has developed a forward plan to develop new standards for protecting the crew during dynamic phases of flight. In collaboration with external peers in industry, academia, and other government agencies, the Team will develop and validate the standards using a combination of data mining, testing, analysis, simulation, and expert opinion. Because all crewmembers must endure dynamic phases of flight, detailed understanding of the human body response to such environments is critical. In addition, because spaceflight-deconditioning causes decreases in bone strength, decreases in muscle strength, and increases in bone fracture risk, the criticality of this understanding is greater with longer duration spaceflight missions.
nasa_hrp_risks.nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Injury from Dynamic Loads
Throughout their missions, astronauts face risks that increase their chances of injury when their vehicles land back on Earth. These risks include gravitational transitions, possible disorientation, and bone loss. Such injuries could significantly affect crew health and mission success. Astronauts moving between different gravitational fields—say, the microgravity of a spacecraft, to the low gravity of the Moon, back to the spacecraft, and then back to Earth—may also have weakened bones and muscles that heighten injury risk.
NASA scientists are building human body models to help characterize how the body is affected in various spaceflight environments. These models help scientists develop the best standards for vehicle designs to reduce injury risks (for instance, standards on seat configurations and the restraints crews use to “strap in” during landing). Researchers are also working to improve the design of spacesuits to better protect astronauts from the forces of spaceflight.
When crews land on Earth, teams are on standby to help them exit their vehicle and perform other postflight activities as they adapt to the return to gravity. But on the Moon and Mars, where there will be varying levels of gravity, crews will need to self-egress and function autonomously shortly after landing – challenges that researchers are working to solve.
Formal risk description: Risk of in-mission injury and performance decrements and long-term health effects from dynamic loads

nasa_hrp_risks.full_title: Risk of Mission Impacts and Long-Term Health Issues due to Decompression Sickness
nasa_hrp_risks.risk_statement: Given that decompression sickness (DCS) is a potential risk for every spaceflight/mission (e.g., EVA or cabin depressurization) and must be mitigated to acceptable risk levels; limitations in quantitative understanding of DCS will lead to conservative DCS risk mitigation countermeasures with significant operational, engineering, and/or secondary health/performance impacts. HSRB State of Knowledge As of today, no reported cases of DCS during flight, yet ground studies with similar decompression stress do cause DCS. Ground studies stop at first symptoms of DCS, so little is known on the progression of DCS symptoms. NASA standards exist for both DCS prevention and treatment and are being incorporated into new programs. Effects of fractional gravity on DCS risk are currently unknown, but will increase the risk compared to microgravity. Current operational pre-breathe (PB) protocols are validated only for the microgravity environment and require hours of PB including multiple procedural steps requiring ground and intravehicular (IV) support to facilitate timing and order of airlock and suit preparation operations. Countermeasure Development: Based on a successful staged decompression to a 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 atmosphere developed for shuttle EVA to reduce prep. time. The 8.2 psia / 34% O2 environment with variable pressure space suit is the recommended approach and is being validated to support an efficient and flexible EVA architecture, however, the ability to implement the Exploration Atmosphere as recommended may be affected by factors including: schedule & budgetary constraints, contract mechanisms, international partnerships, personnel changes, cross-program dependencies, and unanticipated technical challenges. Ability to accurately inform major cross-program architectural decisions is limited by significant uncertainty in unvalidated DCS risk estimation tools. Mitigation Strategy Research tasks associated with understanding, quantifying, and mitigating the risk of DCS during spaceflight are described in the EVA Risk Strategy ( https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/risks/risk.aspx?i=84 ).
nasa_hrp_risks.nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Decompression Sickness
When astronauts move from a pressurized environment like a spacecraft to the lower-pressure environment encountered during spacewalks, health complications can arise due to what’s known as decompression sickness. During decompression sickness, dissolved nitrogen in the bloodstream begins to bubble, which can damage body tissues.
Also known as “the bends,” decompression sickness can occur on Earth when scuba divers attempt to surface too fast. As they quickly ascend, nitrogen gas dissolved in their body tissues rapidly forms bubbles which can cause pain so severe it may force a diver to double over. In severe cases, these bubbles can impact breathing or even block blood vessels and cause stroke-like symptoms.
In space, this same phenomenon can occur when an astronaut moves from a spacecraft to a lower-pressure spacesuit for spacewalks. Spacewalks are one of the highest-risk activities an astronaut will ever do, so decompression sickness is both a health and operational risk.
Earth-based training in both high- and low-pressure environments prior to missions helps astronauts know what to expect in altered pressure situations, including when they might be at risk for decompression sickness. Current protocols hold that when experiencing decompression sickness symptoms, astronauts should safely but rapidly end their spacewalk and return to the pressurized environment of their spacecraft.
Future missions deeper into space will likely require more frequent spacewalks. NASA is preparing for associated risks in a variety of ways. For instance, new variable pressure space suits currently in development may provide some initial ways to address decompression sickness during the spacewalk itself. The suits’ technology aims to allow astronauts to quickly increase the pressure within their suits, which could help stabilize the afflicted crew member and allow for safer return. But astronauts who wear such suits may also experience reduced mobility, decreased manual dexterity, and increased fatigue during spacewalks – since pressurized suits are heavier – so decisions will need to be made about risk tradeoffs.
In addition, the spacecraft for future deep space missions could be designed to operate at lower pressures, helping to limit the pressure changes between habitat and spacesuit, which will reduce risks. nasa_hrp_risks.full_title: Risk of Reduced Crew Health and Performance Due to Hypoxia
nasa_hrp_risks.risk_statement: Given that future human exploration missions require robust, flexible Extravehicular Activity (EVA) architecture protocols that include the use of a reduced pressure cabin atmosphere enabling staged denitrogenation, there is a possibility that this atmosphere could result in compromised health and performance to the crewmember due to exposure to mild hypobaric hypoxia. Notes: - In addition to hypobaric hypoxia associated with staged denitrogenation, there are additional factors that can result in hypoxic exposure to the crewmember such as cabin depressurization, Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) failure, toxic exposure or crewmember illness/injury. - Planned research and countermeasures will focus on mild hypoxia associated with hypoxia related to staged denitrogenation. HSRB State of Knowledge The exploration atmosphere (8.2 psia/34% O2) was selected by the Exploration Atmospheres Working Group (EAWG) because it was considered to be a mildly hypoxic atmosphere with acceptable flammability risk and low O2 prebreathe (PB) overhead to maintain acceptable DCS risk while facilitating efficient EVA operations. The 8.2/34 environment (PI O2 = 128 mmHg) is physiologically similar in terms of O2 availability to the nominal shuttle and ISS staged decompression atmosphere of 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 (PI O2 = 127 mmHg). Both environments provide a hypoxic dose as modeled between 4000-8300 ft altitude. The staged decompression was used on 40 different shuttle missions for durations of 1 to 8 days. Of most concern are the potential effects on the increased intracranial pressure, visual impairment, cognitive performance, sensorimotor dysfunction, oxidative damage and sleep quality. Other areas of focus include incidence and treatment of acute mountain sickness (AMS), development of new exercise countermeasure protocols and effective food preparation at 8.2 psia. Per HLS requirements, the original 7-day limit in NASA-STD-3001 for mildly hypoxic environments was extended to 30 days with monitoring because it was shown to improve the net risk posture for flight crew health and performance. With an agreement on what monitoring is required, this 30-day duration could be extended to indefinite with monitoring for all missions other than Mars, which will need additional assessment due to the long transit in microgravity prior to use of staged denitrogenation environments. Mitigation Strategy Research tasks to investigate physiological responses and mitigating hypoxia risk associated with exposure to hypobaric hypoxic stress as an exploration atmosphere and cycling between mild hypoxia and mild hyperoxia during EVAs is captured under the EVA Risk Strategy ( https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/risks/risk.aspx?i=84 ).

Future missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond will require more frequent spacewalks. But keeping astronauts safe and healthy during any spacewalk currently requires many hours of preparation and a large supply of pure oxygen. Astronauts must inhale pure oxygen over several hours prior to spacewalks to avoid decompression sickness, also known as “the bends.”
To help slash the pure oxygen needs for future frequent spacewalks, NASA’s spacecraft for deep-space missions will have astronauts live and work in a constant partial cabin depressurization (something that now only occurs in the airlock prior to spacewalks). This altered cabin environment will help reduce nitrogen in the body passively.
Yet that partial depressurization will simultaneously increase the risk of mild hypoxia — a condition that occurs when oxygen levels in body tissues become lower than normal. Mild hypoxia, if untreated, can cause confusion, headaches, vision impairment, and trouble sleeping.
NASA’s health experts are researching hypoxia to design protocols that balance oxygen concentration and pressure to optimize astronaut health and performance before and during spacewalks. Creating spacesuits that have the option for crews to be able to toggle pressure increases inside their suits while conducting spacewalks is another area of current research.
No current ground-based study exists to test different oxygen exposure levels on humans while they’re experiencing all the stressors of spaceflight. Instead, scientists are using decades of archived health data on spacewalks to try to extrapolate answers to several questions. For example, will a mildly hypoxic, reduced-pressure environment make any known astronaut health issues worse? If so, what oxygen levels might be tolerable? Scientists are also gathering data from studies conducted in pressure chambers that can simulate spaceflight atmospheres. Studying volunteers that spend hours or days in these chambers allows scientists to learn more about hypoxia and decompression sickness risks and to test potential interventions.
Researchers are using all these areas of research to build new health monitoring protocols and treatment strategies to track how future astronauts will adapt to partial depressurization. These new protocols are being incorporated into medical operations and planning for future missions.

nasa_hrp_risks.full_title: Risk of Adverse Mission Outcomes Due to Earth Independent Human-Systems Operations
nasa_hrp_risks.risk_statement: Given decreasing real-time ground support for execution of Earth independent critical, complex operations during future exploration missions, there is a possibility of adverse performance outcomes, most consequentially that crew are unable to adequately respond to unanticipated critical malfunctions or execute safety-critical procedures. HSRB State of Knowledge Critical malfunctions requiring Crew/Mission Control Center (MCC) management occurred at a rate of 1.7 times per year for International Space Station (ISS) averaged over the lifetime and 3-4 times per year in the burn in phase for the vehicle. These averages do not include EVA data, which greatly increases the incident rate. Prior experience from the Apollo program showed 10/11 crewed missions experienced significant anomalies where crew relied heavily on MCC expertise in real-time. These failure patterns are in line with those observed in other complex engineered systems (e.g., oil rigs, launch systems, commercial aviation, etc.). Mitigation Strategy The Human Systems Integration Architecture (HSIA) risk is comprised of an integrated representation of the Human Factors risk areas of vehicle design and habitability, human computer interaction, human automation and robotics integration, training, and task design. Future deep space missions will present new challenges for crew, and increased risks to human performance due to the stress, fatigue, radiation exposure, and isolation that characterizes these missions. In addition, crew will no longer be able to depend on real-time support from Mission Control due to distance from the Earth, but will have to work increasingly autonomously, performing critical tasks that were previously carried out by Flight Controllers. This greater crew/vehicle autonomy will depend, in part on advanced, on-board automated systems but also on new approaches to training, teaming and crew selection. Most importantly, it will depend on a successful integration of intelligent vehicle capabilities with crew capabilities. Ground laboratories, analogs, and the International Space Station (ISS) are utilized to answer research questions necessary to ensure that future Exploration crewmembers, who will be dealing with many unknowns, communication delays, and increasing autonomy, will be able to adequately perform their tasks and complete their missions. The HSIA risk provides a conceptual framework proposed to address the integration of onboard capability and crew roles and responsibilities necessary to enable crew to respond effectively and efficiently in the required increasing autonomous mission operations framework. Enabling a flight crew of 4 to perform the job that has traditionally been done by a ground crew of 40+ will require a fundamental rethinking of crew-vehicle integration and operations as well as crew-ground collaboration. A flight crew of 4 will need to function more autonomously in response to anticipated reduction in communication quantity and quality as well as unanticipated blackouts instead of depending on frequent real-time communications with a large Mission Control Center (MCC) ground support team of diverse specialties to provide directions (see Dempsey et al., 2018 for a detailed description of the range of support MCC provides). As outlined by Vera and Wu (2018), the impact will be felt particularly in dealing with unanticipated, off-nominal situations. Our current operational models therefore (tied to ground control) must evolve as mission operations become increasingly earth independent. Decreasing real-time ground support for the execution of complex operations during future exploration missions will require the flight crew to respond to potentially safety-critical anomalies with no established procedures on their own. A delay or absence of ground support during unanticipated contingencies can become a significant hazard and increase the risk of jeopardizing crew and vehicle safety if there are not sufficient onboard capabilities to assist with troubleshooting and contingency management. The attainment of increased crew autonomy therefore lies in the ability to complement and enhance crew capabilities so that the 4-person flight crew can, on their own, perform the kind of anomaly response that had previously been done mostly by MCC, and complete these activities in the face of the expected communication delays or unexpected blackouts. It is important to highlight that complex, engineered systems, automated/autonomous or not, will experience unanticipated safety critical malfunctions. These can be due, in part or in whole, to human error and/or space environment impacts, but can also be independent of these. Humans are the critical problem-solving components of complex engineered systems and while Artificial Intelligence, Intelligent/Autonomous Systems can help the human decision maker, especially with pattern analysis, the AI systems will not be able to provide actual problem-solving. Furthermore, reducing the number of crew in any system has the potential to raise risks of non-optimal Human System Integration in unanticipated ways. It is therefore critical that c apabilities be wrapped around the human(s) in order for safety critical issues to be addressable. To further mitigate the risk, specific factors have been identified (e.g., autonomy, anomaly detection and response, etc.) as highly relevant to long duration space missions. Thus, these gaps will focus specifically on understanding the true impact of these factors on long duration missions. At the conclusion of each task, the final report is reviewed and the relevant evidence report is modified or updated to indicate how the results of the research or technology activity address the gaps and contribute to quantifying or mitigating risk or risks. If applicable, the results will also be incorporated into NASA-STD-3001, VOL. II and the Human Integration Design Handbook (HIDH). Evaluations of countermeasure strategies will be made available in the evidence base and recommendations specific to countermeasure implementation for future missions, will also be defined.
nasa_hrp_risks.nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Inadequate Systems Operations Support
NASA’s Mission Control Center trains astronauts to operate various systems on the International Space Station, including ultrasound and computer-based equipment. However, crews still rely on real-time assistance when problems arise. During longer and more distant missions from Earth, crew members will need more extensive training to know how to identify and fix any issues with systems, software, and equipment without real-time support from mission control.
NASA technologists strive to design user-friendly spaceflight systems so that astronauts can perform tasks independently, as needed. Crew members also receive training before a mission to familiarize themselves with various systems and respond to emergencies themselves. NASA researchers continue to work with industry partners and other experts to make spaceflight systems and vehicles easier to operate.
NASA astronauts train, on average, 300 hours in simulators before launch to help familiarize themselves with space vehicles and systems.

nasa_hrp_risks.full_title: Risk of Performance Decrement and Crew Illness Due to Inadequate Food and Nutrition
nasa_hrp_risks.risk_statement: Given that there is a constrained ability to supply adequate food in spaceflight missions, there is a possibility that inadequate nutrition will result in performance decrement, crew illness, and long-term health effects. HSRB State of Knowledge Much is known about the basic nutrition required to maintain performance and health during spaceflight. Standards/controls exist to maintain food safety during spaceflight. Ground data indicates that dehydration and "quicker than usual" weight loss in physically fit individuals will impact cognition and performance. Adequate nutrition and safe food have been demonstrated for 6-month missions and limited 1-year missions that have resupply. Optimizing food/nutrient intake will likely benefit multiple systems, will drive nutrient requirement definitions, and food provisions. There is an uncharacterized risk during LO and LOS missions due to resource restrictions and increased EVAs resulting in reduced food provisioning and preparation capability compared to ISS. The capability to provide safe pre-packaged food with a 5-year shelf life that provides adequate nutrition content, acceptability, safety and variety is a gap. Some countermeasures (CMs) being investigated are: Bioregenerative supplementation and alternative processing, packaging and storage. The impact of both the current and proposed exploration food systems on cognition, performance, behavior, and many other aspects of health is not adequately understood. Potential health impacts include 1) reductions in crew performance (loss of endurance, cognition); 2) crew illness (loss of bone and muscle mass, immune function, cardiovascular performance, gastrointestinal function, severe dehydration, nausea, diarrhea, endocrine function, ocular, psychological health, and the ability to mitigate oxidative damage); 3) long term health effects (cancer, bone, cardio, etc.), 4) interactions with other systems/countermeasures (e.g., drug/nutrient interactions, environment influences on oxidative stress, exercise-induced alterations in energy reqs.). Mitigation Strategy To develop requirements for a nutritious, acceptable/palatable, and safe food system that in addition to providing sustenance can act as a physiological and psychological countermeasure while being balanced with resource constraints.
nasa_hrp_risks.nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
Keeping astronauts’ bodies and minds healthy during space flight requires adequate nutrition . Designing meals for a lengthy mission, however, is a complex undertaking. Scientists need to ensure meals are acceptable, safe, nutritious, long-lasting, easy to prepare, and varied enough to avoid menu fatigue . At the International Space Station, resupply shipments include a small portion of fresh fruits and vegetables, alongside limited shelf-life options like pizza kits. Providing desired foods and extending their shelf-life will become even more complex with longer-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, since food must last longer and be optimized for mass and volume, all without regular resupply shipments.
Significant strides have been made toward improving the space food system over the years, like reducing the sodium content and adding new foods for variety. In preparation for a trip to the Red Planet, NASA researchers are focused on enhancing diets to boost nutritional value, designing a space food system that will meet the needs of a long-duration mission, and testing the food system in long-duration analogs and spaceflight.
Astronauts work with scientists to evaluate and select their preferred foods before their mission. Crew members sample menu items, such as soups, meats, and vegetables. More than 200 foods and beverages are available aboard the space station.
Formal risk description: Risk of performance decrement and crew illness due to inadequate food and nutrition

nasa_hrp_risks.full_title: Risk of Ineffective or Toxic Medications During Long-Duration Exploration Spaceflight
nasa_hrp_risks.risk_statement: Given that there is no current method to sufficiently characterize medication use, drug quality and performance, clinical outcomes, and the impact of a hostile space environment on pharmaceutical stability and potency during long-duration exploration missions, there is a possibility that provision of a safe and effective drug treatment will be significantly limited, impacting crew health and performance. HSRB State of Knowledge FDA standards followed for Low Earth Orbit (LEO) – require frequent up mass (yearly), which will be problematic for some long duration missions and impossible for Mars Preparatory and Planetary DRMs. Effects of spaceflight environmental conditions on medication stability for long-duration and deep space missions are not fully characterized. It is unclear of how, and to what extent, the spaceflight environment and resultant alterations of human physiology may affect drug pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. The potential for drug instability compounded by altered drug response poses a significant risk to exploration crews. Additionally, engineering has concerns about medication/suit compatibility. This affects what medications can be administered to the crew in suited operations. The Human Research Program Element (ExMC) research efforts are underway to propose a safe and effective exploration spaceflight formulary able to maintain a ≥ 3 year shelf-life. The proposed ExMC strategy will provide validation for the chemical / physical pharmaceutical stability, degradation product toxicity, and drug safety profiles, and better characterize pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacotherapeutic properties of drugs in the exploration spaceflight environment. Mitigation Strategy NASA’s current Low Earth Orbit (LEO) operations involve frequent resupply missions that may be problematic for some long duration missions and impossible for deep space exploration missions. As such, ensuring a safe and effective pharmacy for exploration missions is an important challenge. At this time, it is unclear how, and to what extent, 1) the spaceflight environment changes drug stability and 2) alterations of human physiology or the medications themselves affect drug pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. The potential for drug instability compounded by altered drug response may pose a risk to exploration crews. Current research efforts are underway to propose a safe and effective exploration spaceflight formulary able to maintain a ≥ 3 year shelf-life. The proposed ExMC research includes: analysis of medication packaging and storage solutions; studies that will provide validation for chemical / physical pharmaceutical stability; degradation product toxicity and drug safety profiles; and better characterize pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacotherapeutic properties of medications in spaceflight.

nasa_hrp_risks.full_title: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes
nasa_hrp_risks.risk_statement: Given exposure to the spaceflight environment can contribute to cardiovascular deconditioning, dysfunction, and remodeling, there is a possibility that crews will experience impaired performance and adverse cardiovascular health outcomes that necessitate intervention during and after spaceflight and planetary operations. HSRB State of Knowledge Exposure to weightlessness and the resulting headward fluid shift alters blood volume, flow, and pressure, manifesting in changes in vascular and cardiac structure and function (e.g., cardiovascular deconditioning, orthostatic intolerance, decreased exercise capacity). In-mission countermeasures and monitoring have been implemented, and available evidence from current missions in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) suggest that functional impairments recover in the weeks/months after landing with a reconditioning program. Less is known following missions >1 year, and there is minimal experience with missions beyond LEO (>14 days) or in partial gravity (>3 days). Epidemiological evidence does not support an increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease death in astronauts, but mission durations have been limited largely to 4-6 months and there has been limited follow-up. A statistical increase in atherosclerosis-related cardiovascular pathologies are observed at late time points when exposed to ionizing radiation (e.g., gamma-rays and x-rays) at and above 500 milligray (mGy) terrestrially in human. 2018 National Council on Radiation Protection (NCRP) guidance states “there is not sufficient evidence that absorbed doses in the heart ≤0.5 Gy cause CVDs” (in the context of terrestrial radiation protection) and that the underlying mechanisms are still unclear which makes modeling these effects difficult. Age, sleep, exercise, diet, and stress are known contributors to cardiovascular disease. Resource limitations will affect medical capability and clinical outcomes in mission, particularly in missions at a greater distance from Earth. Mitigation Strategy The strategy for understanding and mitigating spaceflight-induced cardiovascular effects is stepwise and includes: 1) Characterization of the effects of long duration weightlessness and radiation exposure, separately and in combination, through experimentation/research and occupational health monitorin g, 2) development , testing and validation of countermeasures in ground, analog, and low-Earth orbit tests, and finally 3) countermeasure validation in the deep spaceflight environment (Gateway and Artemis). To characterize and understand the effects of each spaceflight hazard (altered gravity, radiation, isolation and confinement, hostile closed environment, and distance from Earth) alone and in combination, ground-based analogs, animal models, and human subjects testing will be used (e.g., bed rest, hindlimb suspension, parabolic flight), as well as long-duration spaceflight opportunities to study cells, tissues, animals, and humans exposed to the conditions of LEO. Because experimental radiation studies are generally limited to in-vitro and animal models, the effects of space radiation (thresholds, dose-responses and the effects of chronic or protracted dose-rates) in isolation and in combination with other spaceflight hazards will be characterized using: 1) long-term astronaut occupational surveillance, 2) by leveraging data from human radiotherapy patients and previously flown astronauts of various durations, and 3) by using current and developing new animal, cell culture, and organ-on-a-chip models for ground-based laboratory studies using space radiation analogs (e.g. NSRL). Additionally, monitoring of astronauts during and after Artemis missions also will be conducted. An emerging medical concern is thrombosis during spaceflight, particularly in the internal jugular vein. Though only one case has been documented, it does not preclude that there have been previous cases that were undetected. Characterization of the incidence of thrombosis and definition of the contributing factors that result in a venous thrombus are high priorities. Confirmation or revision of current preflight screening practices, surveillance activities, and interventions as well as development of countermeasures are of great importance to crew health and mission success, particularly for crewed missions beyond Earth orbit. Countermeasures against orthostatic intolerance (OI) are used operationally to protect crew upon return to Earth, but whether countermeasures are required to protect the crew during head-to-foot accelerations experienced during descent to and ascent from an extraterrestrial surface is not defined. An investigation of OI in males and females with and without lower body compression garments during varying simulated gravity levels is ongoing . The results of this study will help inform the standards and requirements defining the acceleration limits for the Human Landing System Program with and without compression garment and whether additional OI countermeasures may be needed. Candidate c ountermeasure identification and development for non-orthostatic intolerance concerns rely upon data mining, monitoring emerging research and developments highlighted at conferences, literature review, the NASA process of Request for Information (RFI), studies using human iPSCs (human-induced pluripotent stem cell), and workshops and technical interchange meetings (TIM) with key experts. Countermeasure testing will be conducted on the ground in established animal models and human subject-relevant spaceflight analogs followed by demonstration of countermeasure efficacy in ISS astronauts. Data collection on astronauts during and after Artemis missions using the suggested countermeasures will complete the mitigation strategy.
nasa_hrp_risks.nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations
Low-gravity conditions and other spaceflight stressors can alter the heart and blood vessels , potentially leading to blood clots, heart arrythmias, cardiovascular disease, and low blood pressure which elevates the chances of fainting at landing. The risk of developing these conditions will increase with longer-duration missions such as a multi-year trip to Mars, so research focused on understanding and treating these risks is a priority for NASA.
Regular exercise and healthy diets help crews maintain cardiovascular fitness. Lower-body compression garments and drinking lots of fluids prior to landing can help to prevent low blood pressure. For future Mars missions, astronauts will also receive enhanced training to respond to cardiovascular emergencies.
Low gravity can also physically change the shape of the human heart , making it become more spherical.
Formal risk description: Risk of cardiovascular adaptations contributing to adverse mission performance and health outcomes

nasa_hrp_risks.full_title: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness
nasa_hrp_risks.risk_statement: Given that exposure to a reduced gravity environment causes cardio-respiratory (e.g., maximal oxygen consumption and ventilatory threshold) and musculoskeletal fitness (e.g., strength, power, and endurance) to decline, there is a risk of impaired mission task performance and adverse health outcomes. Note: This risk is carried as two separate risks at the HSRB. The content in this field has been developed by HRP. HSRB State of Knowledge Despite the use of inflight exercise countermeasures on the International Space Station (ISS), current evidence suggests that cardio-respiratory and musculoskeletal fitness decrease during spaceflight and after spaceflight, though individual variability is evident that cannot be fully explained by countermeasure adherence. During ISS missions, some astronauts do not meet the current fitness standards for operations in weightlessness, and many astronauts would not meet current fitness standards for extravehicular operations on celestial surfaces. Further, many have not returned to preflight fitness levels by the end of the standard reconditioning program (30 days after landing). Limited data exist for astronauts who participate in spaceflight missions greater than the standard ISS mission duration (4-6 months), for women astronauts, and during and after partial gravity exposures. In long-duration missions on ISS, astronauts have access for a robust suite of exercise countermeasures (cycle ergometer, treadmill, resistive exercise) but countermeasure capabilities likely will be reduced for exploration missions due to mass, volume, and power limitations. As the design and architecture of future exploration missions evolve (e.g., vehicle design, spacesuit design, mission objectives), characterization of physical requirements to perform critical tasks and of crew health in these novel mission scenarios is required to inform and refine the requirements for countermeasures against cardio-respiratory and musculoskeletal deconditioning and the physical fitness standards which these countermeasures are intended to support. Note: This risk is carried as two separate risks at the HSRB. The content in this field has been developed by HRP. Mitigation Strategy Extended duration spaceflight mission studies and evaluations of novel exercise systems on ISS, Orion, and Gateway as well as in spaceflight or ground analogs are planned to help inform this risk for exploration class missions, including Mars mission parameters. EVA task-specific evaluations will include assessment of the fitness levels required to successfully perform mission tasks. This includes measuring metabolic costs and muscle strength requirements of critical tasks and of individual factors contributing to task success (e.g., anthropometry, hydration and caloric intake, fatigue, and sex). Operational Relevance: If muscle and/or cardio-respiratory fitness are below levels required to perform mission critical tasks then the crew are at higher risks for compromised performance capabilities. The compromised capabilities could impact the ability to complete mission objectives and result in decreased mission efficiency and efficacy, or increased risk for injury or other health impacts. Programs need to provide adequate exercise systems and time to perform the exercise to maintain performance capabilities across all phases of the mission (pre-, in-, and post-flight). HRP needs to provide the SME knowledge and contribute to the data needs to develop programmatic exercise system requirements.
nasa_hrp_risks.nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness
Living in microgravity can weaken the bones, muscles, and cardiopulmonary systems of astronauts, making it difficult for them to carry out critical mission tasks while also increasing the risk of injury. These physiological changes can make falling or tripping more likely, especially during gravitational transitions to the surface of the Moon or Mars, or when returning to their daily living on Earth.
Six to seven days a week, astronauts on the International Space Station perform resistance training and aerobic exercises for 1.5 hours per day to maintain their fitness and protect against muscle and bone loss. Crew members also undergo periodic fitness self-evaluations to help researchers monitor their health and fitness and to optimize the astronauts’ training regimen. Spacecraft set to carry astronauts to the Moon and Mars, however, will likely have less space for exercise equipment. Consequently, researchers are working to understand how to optimize both exercise machines and protocols to ensure that astronaut health is maintained on these deep space missions.
The effects of exposure to microgravity can vary substantially between individual astronauts. However, data from International Space Station missions indicates that average losses to strength and aerobic fitness are 10-12% of pre-mission levels. Depending on how it’s measured, between 12-38% of space station crew members lose more than 20% of their pre-mission fitness. Strength loss affects a larger proportion of crew members than does the decline in aerobic fitness. Losses are seen across physical performance areas, including upper and lower body strength and endurance, flexibility, aerobic fitness, agility, and coordination.
Formal risk description: Risk of mission performance decrements and adverse health outcomes resulting from reduced cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness

csa_resources.title: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?
csa_resources.full_text:
Science is our quest for more knowledge about the world and ourselves. For thousands of years, humanity has pushed boundaries in its search to learn more about our place in the universe.
Canadian science on the International Space Station
Canada's participation in the International Space Station ( ISS ) allows our scientists to access the unique space environment and conduct cutting-edge experiments aboard the orbiting laboratory to:
prepare for deep-space destinations
use the knowledge obtained to improve our quality of life on Earth
Did you know that many science experiments are being conducted on the ISS at any given time? Why do we do science in space? (Credit: Canadian Space Agency) ( Transcript )
Preparing for deep-space destinations
As space agencies from all over the world are looking to propel humanity further into the solar system, Canada's space science community continues to conduct research aboard the ISS .
We want to better understand the risks associated with human space flight—and help find countermeasures and treatments—to identify, characterize, and mitigate the effects on astronauts' health in order to make space travel safer.
Missions to the Moon and Mars mean longer trips and more risks for astronauts, including:
more time in weightlessness
more exposure to radiation
longer periods of isolation, very far from home
increased delays in communication with Earth
less ability to rely on Earth for food, materials, and emergency medical assistance
Using the knowledge obtained to improve our quality of life on Earth
Studying the way our body changes in space help us understand the impacts of reduced levels of physical activity and issues that affect older adult populations on Earth.
Living in weightless conditions changes the human body in many ways. The effects observed in astronauts are similar to accelerated aging and health problems caused by a sedentary lifestyle . Studying the human body in space for six months gives us data that would take years to gather on Earth. New information gained in space contributes to improved quality of life on Earth .
Canadian scientists use space to study our bones, heart, blood vessels and brain. Their experiments have produced findings that can help people suffering from balance problems , such as seniors; osteoporosis ; cardiovascular disorders; and Type-2 diabetes .

csa_resources.title: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health
csa_resources.full_text:
Canadian Space Agency ( CSA ) astronaut David Saint-Jacques using bubble detectors, a predecessor to Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS), on the International Space Station ( ISS ). (Credits: CSA / NASA )
Radiation is one of the key challenges faced by astronauts living and working beyond the protective shield of Earth’s atmosphere. As Canada and its international partners advance plans for missions to the Moon, and eventually Mars, the CSA continues to invest in technology to better understand exposure levels.
The CSA has awarded a contract of $5.5 million to Bubble Technology Industries for the continued development of the CANS , a compact and autonomous instrument designed to measure neutron radiation exposure in space.
Neutron radiation, which contributes to about 30% of total radiation on the ISS , is especially harmful because it can cause serious biological damage and require specialized protective measures. For over 25 years, the ISS has been a test bed for new technology. Canada has significant expertise in radiation detection experiments on the ISS , including MOSFET , EVARM and Radi-N and Radi-N2 .
CANS improves upon previous radiation detection methods with the unique combined capabilities of working continuously and autonomously. Data collected could help develop better measures to reduce risks for astronauts’ health and also has potential applications on Earth, including cancer therapy, radiation protection for aircrews, nuclear threat detection and public safety, among others.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Blood Glucose (Fasting / Pre-Post Exercise)
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Unloading of postural muscles (soleus/quadriceps) reduces GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake and induces spaceflight-associated insulin resistance.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Finger-prick micro-glucometer or wearable continuous interstitial glucose sensor; verified via Inspiration4 CMP (OSD-575).
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Daily high-intensity ergometer + ARED resistance workouts; balanced low-glycemic spaceflight nutrition; hydration check.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Arterial Blood Pressure (Systolic / Diastolic)
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Cephalad fluid shift (1.5-2 L from legs to thorax/head) raises upper-body vascular pressure in orbit and causes post-flight orthostatic intolerance.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Oscillometric arm cuff held strictly at heart level while stationary for 60s; Doppler ultrasound for jugular flow.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) device, fluid-loading electrolyte protocol before re-entry, aerobic cycling.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Resting Heart Rate
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Cardiac remodeling, reduced plasma volume (10-15%), and altered autonomic baroreflex sensitivity increase arrhythmia/tachycardia risk.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: 12-lead ECG, chest-strap telemetry, or optical PPG wearable; linked to radiation cardiac studies (OSD-435).
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Daily cardiovascular ergometer conditioning, electrolyte balance, 12-lead ECG uplink during chest pain/palpitations.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Core Body Temperature
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Absence of convective cooling and sweat pooling causes 'Space Fever' (+0.5 to +1.0°C baseline elevation during exercise/rest).
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Temporal artery forehead thermometer or ingestible telemetry pill.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Increase cabin airflow fans, liquid-cooling ventilation garment (LCVG) during EVA, check infection/latent viral reactivation.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO2)
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Mild hypoxemia risks during EVA prebreathe, decompression events, or Lunar/Mars reduced-pressure habitat atmospheres (8.2 psi / 34% O2).
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Fingertip pulse oximetry + cabin PPO2/CO2 ECLSS telemetry.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Immediate supplemental O2 (4 L/min), verify cabin O2/CO2 scrubbers, screen for decompression sickness (DCS) symptoms.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Daily Sleep Duration & Circadian Alignment
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: 16 orbital sunrises/sunsets per 24h, cabin noise, CO2 pockets, and workload shifts cause chronic sleep debt and circadian desynchronization.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Wrist actigraphy, sleep logs, and PVT cognitive reaction testing.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Blue-enriched morning / amber evening solid-state lighting, sleep-station airflow fans, CBT-I & scheduled wind-down.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Behavioral Health & Mood Score (PHQ-9 / Stress Scale)
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Prolonged isolation, confinement, crew friction, and communication delay (>22 min one-way to Mars) elevate anxiety, depression, and cognitive fatigue.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Self-report mood check-ins, speech/facial affect biomarkers, and computerized cognitive batteries.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Private family audio/video conferences, autonomous psychological support tools, workload balancing, structured recreation.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Postural Stability & Sensorimotor Balance Score
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Otolith unloading and proprioceptive reweighting cause space motion sickness in orbit and severe postural ataxia upon gravity transitions (Moon/Mars/Earth).
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Computerized MediaPipe Pose sway kinematics, tandem walk, and sit-to-stand balance tests.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Vestibular adaptation exercises, handrail anchoring, Promethazine for acute SMS, sensorimotor reconditioning before EVA.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Bilateral Joint Kinematics Symmetry Difference
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Asymmetric musculoskeletal deconditioning, EVA suit shoulder/hand strain, or intervertebral disc swelling (spinal elongation) causes kinematic asymmetry.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Real-time pose landmark joint angle symmetry (left vs right shoulder, hip, knee) via onboard camera.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Balanced ARED resistance loading, spinal decompression stretching, EVA suit fit verification.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Ocular Fatigue (EAR) & SANS Neuro-Ocular Status
clinical_indicators_thresholds.critical_threshold: EAR < 0.195 or IOP > 22 mmHg / acute visual acuity drop
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Headward fluid shift elevates intracranial/choroidal pressure, causing optic disc edema, globe flattening, choroidal folds, and hyperopic shift (SANS).
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: FaceMesh Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR) for fatigue + In-flight OCT, Fundoscopy, Tonometry IOP, and ocular ultrasound (OSD-583/679).
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: LBNP fluid redistribution, B-vitamin/one-carbon metabolic supplementation, corrective Space Anticipation Glasses, OCT tracking.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Space Radiation Dose Rate & Cumulative Exposure (GCR / SPE / Neutrons)
clinical_indicators_thresholds.critical_threshold: > 50 mSv/hr (SPE Solar Particle Event) or > 600 mSv career limit
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: GCR high-Z/energy ions and secondary neutrons (~30% of ISS dose per CSA CANS) damage DNA, elevate lifetime cancer risk, and injure CNS/cardiovascular tissue.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Active dosimeters (RAD), CSA Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS), Radi-N2 bubble detectors, crew personal badges.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Retreat to Aft Water Wall / polyethylene storm shelter during SPE, abort EVA within 8 min, log personal dosimeter rates.

clinical_indicators_thresholds.name: Cabin CO2 Partial Pressure (ppCO2)
clinical_indicators_thresholds.microgravity_effect: Closed ECLSS habitats accumulate CO2 pockets around crew without airflow, causing headaches, cognitive impairment, hypercapnia, and exacerbating SANS.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.measurement_in_space: Continuous ECLSS CO2 infrared analyzers + transcutaneous pCO2 monitoring.
clinical_indicators_thresholds.countermeasure: Verify CDRA/amine scrubber status, maximize sleep-station ventilation fans, inspect filters for lunar/martian dust.

body_systems_matrix.hazards: Gravity Fields, Space Radiation, Isolation and Confinement, Hostile/Closed Environments
body_systems_matrix.key_conditions: Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), Vestibular Ataxia / Space Motion Sickness, Cognitive/Sleep Decrement, Hypercapnia
body_systems_matrix.measurable_indicators: Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR), Intraocular Pressure (IOP), OCT Retinal/Choroidal Thickness, Sleep Hours, Mood Score, Balance Score
body_systems_matrix.prevention_and_treatment: In-flight OCT & tonometry, LBNP fluid shift countermeasures, circadian lighting, Promethazine for acute SMS, CO2 scrubbing.

body_systems_matrix.hazards: Gravity Fields, Space Radiation, Hostile/Closed Environments
body_systems_matrix.key_conditions: Orthostatic Intolerance, Cardiac Remodeling, Venous Thromboembolism (Jugular Stasis), Radiation-Induced CVD, Decompression Sickness
body_systems_matrix.measurable_indicators: Systolic/Diastolic BP, Resting Heart Rate, 12-Lead ECG, SpO2, Echocardiography, Serum CRP/Fibrinogen
body_systems_matrix.prevention_and_treatment: Daily aerobic ergometer + resistance exercise, pre-landing fluid loading, LBNP, Doppler jugular ultrasound, O2 prebreathe before EVA.

body_systems_matrix.key_conditions: Bone Mineral Density Loss (1-1.5%/month), Muscle Atrophy, Intervertebral Disc Herniation/Back Pain, EVA Joint Injury
body_systems_matrix.measurable_indicators: Bilateral Joint Symmetry Diff, Posture Balance Score, Grip/Muscle Force, Vitamin D & Calcium, Serum ALP
body_systems_matrix.prevention_and_treatment: ARED high-load resistive exercise (2+ hrs/day), bisphosphonates/Vitamin D, balanced protein nutrition, spinal unloading stretches.

body_systems_matrix.hazards: Space Radiation, Isolation and Confinement, Hostile/Closed Environments, Distance from Earth
body_systems_matrix.key_conditions: Immune Dysregulation & Latent Viral Reactivation, Insulin Resistance, Altered Drug Pharmacokinetics, Radiation Carcinogenesis
body_systems_matrix.measurable_indicators: Blood Glucose, Body Temp ('Space Fever'), WBC/Lymphocyte/Neutrophil CBC, Metabolic Panel (CMP), Cytokines, Radiation mSv
body_systems_matrix.prevention_and_treatment: In-flight CBC/CMP blood/saliva/urine assays, radiation shielding/storm shelters, microbiome hygiene, stability-tested medical formulary.

body_systems_matrix.key_conditions: Renal Stone Formation (Hypercalciuria from bone resorption + dehydration)
body_systems_matrix.measurable_indicators: BUN, Creatinine, eGFR, Serum/Urine Calcium, Daily Hydration Volume
body_systems_matrix.prevention_and_treatment: Potassium citrate prophylaxis, >= 2.5 L/day fluid intake, renal ultrasound monitoring.

steps: Anchor crew member to primary handrails to prevent rotational tumble and head impact.
Restrict rapid head movements in pitch and yaw axes (mitigate Coriolis effect).
Administer Promethazine 25mg IM or oral if accompanied by active space motion sickness (SMS).
Inspect cabin air intake filters for particulate, Lunar/Mars dust, or chemical irritants.

steps: Immediately sound habitat klaxon: all crew retreat to Aft Water Wall / polyethylene storm shelter.
Terminate ongoing Extravehicular Activities (EVA) within 8-minute airlock contingency window.
Record active personal dosimeter (RAD) and CSA CANS neutron spectrometer readings immediately.
Deploy auxiliary polyethylene shielding blankets over crew bunk positions.
Await Space Radiation Analysis Group (SRAG) real-time flux clearance before resuming EVA.

steps: Don emergency 100% O2 mask or seal EVA suit pressure loop immediately.
Verify cabin total pressure, PPO2, and ppCO2 on ECLSS console.
If DCS suspected post-EVA, initiate hyperbaric treatment protocol (suit/airlock repressurization + 100% O2).
Log neurological exam, pulse oximetry, and vital signs every 5 minutes.
